subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A second-year student is reviewing the embryologic gut regions and their arterial and neural supply for an anatomy examination. She is specifically asked about the portion of bowel extending from the distal third of the transverse colon to the upper anal canal.
question: Which combination of artery, parasympathetic innervation, and vertebral level correctly matches this gut region?

options.text: Celiac artery; vagus nerve; T12-L1.
Superior mesenteric artery; vagus nerve; L1.
Inferior mesenteric artery; pelvic splanchnic nerves; L3.
Inferior mesenteric artery; vagus nerve; L1.
Celiac artery; pelvic splanchnic nerves; L3.

explanation_correct: The hindgut extends from the distal one-third of the transverse colon to the upper portion of the anal canal. It is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery, receives parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves, and is referenced at the L3 vertebral level. Sympathetic fibers to the hindgut pass through the inferior mesenteric prevertebral ganglion.

explanation_incorrect.A: That combination describes the foregut, which extends from the pharynx to the proximal duodenum and includes the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen.
explanation_incorrect.B: That combination describes the midgut, from the distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
explanation_incorrect.D: The IMA is correct for the hindgut, but parasympathetic supply there is from pelvic splanchnic nerves, not the vagus; L1 is the midgut level.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pelvic splanchnic nerves and L3 fit the hindgut, but the artery for that region is the IMA rather than the celiac artery.

educationalObjective: Hindgut: IMA, pelvic splanchnic parasympathetics, L3, from the distal third of the transverse colon to the upper anal canal.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 47-year-old woman is being evaluated for upper abdominal pain. Her surgeon reviews which organs fall within the foregut territory before planning endoscopy and imaging. The review emphasizes that the foregut includes mesoderm-derived organs in addition to the portions of the digestive tube itself.
question: Which of the following structures belongs entirely to the foregut (celiac artery) territory of the GI blood supply table?

options.text: Distal duodenum and proximal jejunum.
Proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
Descending colon and upper portion of the anal canal.
Lower esophagus, which receives both celiac arterial and vagal supply.
Liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen.

explanation_correct: The foregut is supplied by the celiac trunk with vagal parasympathetic input at T12-L1. It runs from the pharynx to the proximal duodenum and includes the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen, which are mesoderm-derived associated organs. The pharynx receives vagal innervation only, whereas the lower esophagus receives celiac arterial supply only.

explanation_incorrect.A: The distal duodenum and jejunum are midgut structures supplied by the SMA with vagal innervation at L1.
explanation_incorrect.B: The proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon is the distal limit of the midgut, not the foregut.
explanation_incorrect.C: The descending colon and upper anal canal are hindgut structures supplied by the IMA and pelvic splanchnic nerves.
explanation_incorrect.D: The lower esophagus receives celiac artery supply only; vagal innervation is listed for the pharynx, so this option does not match the table.

educationalObjective: Foregut means celiac artery and vagus at T12-L1, covering the pharynx to proximal duodenum plus liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 61-year-old man has a tumor at the celiac axis encasing the main arterial trunk to the foregut. Before surgical resection, the vascular team reviews which vessels arise directly from that trunk so they can preserve collateral flow to the stomach, liver, and spleen.
question: Which three arteries are the direct branches of the celiac trunk?

options.text: Common hepatic, splenic, and left gastric arteries.
Proper hepatic, splenic, and right gastric arteries.
Left gastric, gastroduodenal, and inferior mesenteric arteries.
Common hepatic, superior mesenteric, and left gastroepiploic arteries.
Splenic, cystic, and right gastric arteries.

explanation_correct: The celiac trunk classically divides into the common hepatic, splenic, and left gastric arteries, which together constitute the main blood supply of the foregut. The proper hepatic and gastroduodenal arteries are distal branches of the common hepatic; the left gastroepiploic artery arises from the splenic artery; and the right gastric and cystic arteries are smaller distal branches.

explanation_incorrect.B: The proper hepatic and right gastric arteries are distal branches, not direct celiac branches; only the splenic artery in this list is a primary branch.
explanation_incorrect.C: The gastroduodenal artery arises from the common hepatic artery and the inferior mesenteric artery comes directly off the aorta, so neither is a celiac branch.
explanation_incorrect.D: The superior mesenteric artery is a separate aortic branch and the left gastroepiploic artery comes from the splenic artery, not the celiac trunk itself.
explanation_incorrect.E: The cystic artery usually arises from the right hepatic artery and the right gastric artery is a distal vessel; only the splenic artery is a direct celiac branch here.

educationalObjective: The celiac trunk gives off the common hepatic, splenic, and left gastric arteries to supply the foregut.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 54-year-old woman with a bleeding gastric ulcer undergoes angiography. The radiologist notes that even if one of the major named vessels to the stomach is compromised, significant collateral flow can still reach the gastric wall through two paired arterial arcades.
question: Which two anastomoses provide these strong collateral pathways around the stomach?

options.text: Left and right colic arteries; left and right gastric arteries.
Left and right gastroepiploic arteries; left and right gastric arteries.
Short gastric arteries and gastroduodenal artery.
Superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries; left and right gastroepiploic arteries.
Common hepatic and splenic arteries alone.

explanation_correct: Strong anastomoses exist between the left and right gastroepiploic arteries along the greater curvature and between the left and right gastric arteries along the lesser curvature. These connections form the principal collateral circulation of the stomach, linking celiac-derived and SMA-derived flow.

explanation_incorrect.A: Left and right colic arteries are colic vessels; only the left and right gastric anastomosis is one of the two strong gastric collaterals.
explanation_incorrect.C: Short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery and the gastroduodenal artery from the common hepatic artery, but they are not the paired named arcades described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: The pancreaticoduodenal arcades supply the duodenum and pancreas; only the gastroepiploic pair belongs to the stomach's collateral network.
explanation_incorrect.E: The common hepatic and splenic arteries are proximal celiac branches, not the two gastric arcades that anastomose with each other.

educationalObjective: The stomach's strong collateral anastomoses are left-right gastroepiploic and left-right gastric.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 58-year-old man has a tumor in the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. The oncology team is mapping the arterial supply and parasympathetic pathway for the planned segmental resection. A second lesion in the distal third of the transverse colon is being followed separately.
question: Which artery and parasympathetic supply serve the segment containing the main tumor?

options.text: Inferior mesenteric artery and pelvic splanchnic nerves (L3).
Celiac artery and vagus nerve (T12-L1).
Superior mesenteric artery and pelvic splanchnic nerves (L1).
Superior mesenteric artery and vagus nerve (L1).
Inferior mesenteric artery and vagus nerve (L3).

explanation_correct: The midgut extends from the distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. It is supplied by the SMA and receives parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve, corresponding to the L1 level; sympathetic input relays through the superior mesenteric prevertebral ganglion. The distal third of the transverse colon marks the transition to hindgut (IMA, pelvic splanchnic nerves, L3).

explanation_incorrect.A: That combination applies to the hindgut, which begins at the distal one-third of the transverse colon rather than the proximal two-thirds.
explanation_incorrect.B: The celiac artery and vagus at T12-L1 supply the foregut, ending at the proximal duodenum, far proximal to the transverse colon.
explanation_incorrect.C: The SMA is correct for this midgut segment, but parasympathetic innervation here is vagal; pelvic splanchnic nerves serve the hindgut.
explanation_incorrect.E: This mismatches the pairs: vagal fibers do not accompany the IMA, and the IMA supplies the distal third of the transverse colon onward.

educationalObjective: Midgut (distal duodenum to proximal two-thirds of transverse colon) is SMA plus vagus at L1; the distal third switches to IMA plus pelvic splanchnics at L3.
